newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel firm on EMU targets, gold doubts grow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel firm on EMU targets, gold doubts grow.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday stressed the need for strict adherence to European single currency convergence targets even as a fellow EU finance minister cast doubt on German plans to reduce its deficit.
Waigel warned against lax interpretation of the Maastricht entry criteria, and added that talk of a delay to European economic and monetary union (EMU) was damaging.

Speculation about a delay to EMU heightened again after Germany, which is battling with high unemployment and a gaping hole in its budget deficit, said last week that it planned to revalue central bank gold reserves to plug the deficit gap.

The controversial announcement prompted cries of 'fudge' and 'creative accounting' from some European quarters and many independent analysts said it smacked of desperation on the part of the German government.
Belgian finance minister Phillipe Maystadt joined the debate on Thursday, telling reporters in Brussels he could not see how Germany could use central bank reserves to reduce the deficit.
"I don't see how it is possible to translate the revaluation to a reduction in public deficits," he said.

He added, however, that there was a possibility that the European Union's statistical office Eurostat would approve Germany's proposals, meaning that such moves would also be allowed for other EMU hopefuls.

Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert, speaking in Leipzig on Thursday, said he was sure the Maastricht deficit target, which calls on countries wishing to join EMU to bring deficits to within three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), would be met legitimately.
"I am confident that the three percent goal can be reached in a manner which fully complies with the rules," Sievert said.
He said gold revaluation returns could be classified in the same way as tax returns and extraordinary Bundesbank profits.

The Bundesbank currently books its assets at their all-time lowest price, or at the purchase price. Analysts say Waigel's proposed gold revaluation could deliver a one-off profit of up to 40 billion marks ($23.6 billion) for state funds.

Confusion about how and if Waigel's revaluation plans could help Germany's fiscal position is likely to continue until next Wednesday, when the government has said it will release more details of the proposals.

Some analysts said the revaluation could be transferred to the government as an extraordinary profit transfer from the Bundesbank, while others said any profits realised would only directly affect national debt, taking only limited pressure off the deficit in the form of reduced interest payments.
The government, in any case, is resolutely sticking to its forecast for a 2.9 deficit to GDP ratio this year, although many economists said a figure of between 3.2 and 3.5 percent was more likely.

Waigel said Bonn, which has already said it is considering to sell off some of its Deutsche Telekom shares in another attempt to raise extra cash, also planned to step up the pace of privatisation in Germany over the next two years.
He also said he expected stronger growth, higher tax revenues and lower unemployment levels next year.
